Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

after conjunction

after he came: the conjunction

also after (doing), once, when (after)

classical

Hor. S. 2.8.57–58: postquam nihil esse perīclī sēnsimus, ērigimur
Verg. A. 1.216: postquam exēmpta famēs epulīs mēnsaeque remōtae
Traupman 269

postquam

conjunction, with the perfect indicative where English has the pluperfect

after, when

“After he had come” is postquam vēnit: Latin uses the perfect, as with ubi and ut. Written apart with a measure of time: post … quam, so many days after.

Other words

  • ablātīvus absolūtus — after (doing), when … had been done

    a noun and a participle in the ablative · also used · classical · Varr. RR 3.16.35: quō factō nōn modo dēsistunt pugnā

    The usual Latin for “after doing X” or “when X was done”, with no conjunction: quō factō, after which; cēnā factā, after dinner. Lewis & Short has the grammarians’ ablātīvus; the name of the construction is modern.

Examples

  • postquam nihil esse perīclī sēnsimus, ērigimur

    once we see there is no danger, we sit up againHor. S. 2.8.57–58

  • postquam exēmpta famēs epulīs mēnsaeque remōtae

    after hunger was taken away by the feast and the tables removedVerg. A. 1.216

  • haec postquam omnia sēcrēvimus, tum suō quaeque locō disposuimus

    after we had sorted all these things, we put each in its placeCol. 12.3.3

  • quae crēbrius inter sē pugnābunt, aspargī eās oportet aquā mulsā. quō factō nōn modo dēsistunt pugnā, sed etiam conferciunt sē lingentēs

    the bees that keep fighting should be sprinkled with honey-water; after that they not only stop fighting but crowd together licking one anotherVarr. RR 3.16.35

See also before, when, as soon as, then.
